title: Take my hand: the whispered word was karma
hookLine: asked what's left of a person after death, Yajnavalkya takes his questioner's hand, walks him out, and talks about karma
carry: karma: you become what you do
tomorrow: a spirit told him where the lost kings went. does Yajnavalkya know?

cards: The second challenger is Artabhaga, and his last question is one people still ask.

When a person dies, he says, their speech goes into fire, their breath into the wind, their eye into the sun, their mind into the moon, their body into the earth, their hair into the plants and trees, their blood into the waters.
Then where is that person? And this time, Yajnavalkya won't answer in front of the crowd. Artabhaga, my friend, he says.
Take my hand. This is for the two of us alone.

teach.b: Artabhaga's questions start dry. How many graspers are there, and how many over-graspers? Eight, Yajnavalkya says.
The tongue grasps, and taste grasps it back. The eye grasps, and form grabs the eye. Everything we take hold of takes hold of us.

teach.h: WHAT DOES NOT LEAVE? THE NAME.
teach.b: When a person dies, what does not leave them? The name, Yajnavalkya says. The name is endless.

Then the last question, where is the person when everything has gone back, and the hand, and the walk out of the room. The text tells us only this about their private talk. What they talked about was karma.

teach.h: GOOD BY GOOD ACTION, BAD BY BAD.
teach.b: A person becomes good by good action, and bad by bad action. And Artabhaga fell silent. Karma means action, the thing you do, and it had been a word of the ritual: the rite done right.
Here two people step outside and talk about it as the thread of a life, carried past death.
Some readers hear in it an early statement of the teaching Hindus still live by: you become what you do. Not luck, not cosmic revenge. Each action shapes the one who does it, and the shaping goes on.
Why whisper it? The text doesn't say. Perhaps it was too serious for a contest.
So when a classroom laughs that karma got someone, a Hindu teacher might gently turn it around: karma is less about what happens to them, and more about what your own actions are making of you.

how: Hindus remember the dead by name in shraddha rites, offering food and water to ancestors named in a family line; teachers of the Upanishads point to Artabhaga's dialogue as an early statement of karma.

s: Yajnavalkya answers every question in the debate in public
Artabhaga's last one he answers privately: take my hand.
it means action; earlier it was used for the ritual act.
Yajnavalkya says the name does not leave a person at death
the name is endless, he says.

games.q: Artabhaga asks: when everything in a dead person has gone back to fire, wind, sun and earth, where is that person? what does Yajnavalkya's private answer point to?
o: karma: what the person did, and what it made of them.
the body, kept whole in another world.
games.why: they talked about karma and praised karma: a person becomes good by good action, bad by bad. what you do is what carries on.

practice: Hindu families say their ancestors' names at shraddha, the rite for the dead. Bring to mind someone who has died, someone you knew or only heard of, and say their name silently.
Notice it still brings a face, a voice, a way of doing things. Then let one thing they did come to mind, good or ordinary, and hold the name and the action together.

wordCard.voice: Artabhaga. The questioner Yajnavalkya took aside, and the word the two of them praised in private: karma, action, the thing you do, and what it makes of you.

orig.note: Sanskrit karma (stem karman), from kṛ, to do: action, deed, and in the Vedas the ritual act.

carryVoice: Keep this one: karma, you become what you do. Tomorrow, a challenger brings a question he heard from a spirit. That's day three hundred seventy-three.
